readerTitle: What Dropbox's famous demo video really tested
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Dropbox, 2007~2008년 데모 영상) + 가상 적용 (접이식 물류 상자 제조사)
insight: 데모는 '사람들이 원하는가'만 시험한다. Dropbox 영상은 제품 개발을 대신한 것이 아니라, 만들기와 나란히 수요라는 다른 가정을 시험했다.
misconception: 제품을 만들지 말고 영상부터 만들면 된다. 대기자 명단이 길면 사업이 된다는 뜻이다.

sources.text: Ries, E. (2011). The Lean Startup. Crown Business. Dropbox 데모 영상과 대기자 명단 증가(약 5,000명→약 75,000명)에 대한 Drew Houston의 설명 인용
Drew Houston, "Dropbox: Startup Lessons Learned" 발표 (Startup Lessons Learned Conference, 2010). 기존 대안(이메일, USB)과 설명하기 어려운 제품이라는 문제
Dropbox, Inc. Form S-1 (SEC, 2018). 이후 상장 기업으로 성장했다는 사실 확인용

factChecks.note: 대기자 명단 5,000명→75,000명 '하룻밤 사이' 수치는 The Lean Startup에 인용된 Houston 본인의 설명입니다. 독립 검증 수치가 아니므로 카드에 'by Houston's account'로 적었습니다. 원문 표현을 게시 전 확인하세요.
영상 시기: 첫 데모 영상은 2007년(Y Combinator 지원·Hacker News 공개), Digg를 겨냥한 영상은 2008년 초로 알려져 있습니다. 카드에는 '2008'과 'a later version'으로만 적었습니다. 날짜를 다시 확인하세요.
영상 속 소프트웨어가 실제로 작동하는 초기 버전이었다는 점은 Houston의 발표와 Ries의 서술에 근거합니다. 영상에 '내부 농담'이 많았다는 점도 Ries의 서술이며, 구체적인 농담 내용은 적지 않았습니다.
2번 카드의 상황 설명(2007년, 사람들이 이메일·USB로 충분하다고 반응)은 Houston 발표 내용을 일반적으로 요약한 것이며 선택지는 가상입니다. 8번 카드 상자 제조사는 전부 가상 사례이며 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: What Dropbox's famous demo video really tested
body: In 2008, a short video showed files quietly syncing from one computer to another. The product was still in private beta.
It became one of the most retold stories in startups: test your idea before you build it. The usual retelling skips the most useful part.

image.label: A laptop screen showing a short demo video of files syncing
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 노트북 화면에 재생 중인 영상 플레이어, 화면 안에서 파일 아이콘이 다른 컴퓨터로 날아가는 모습. 화면 옆에 사람 아이콘이 점점 길어지는 줄. 실제 Dropbox 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your product is hard to explain.
body: It's 2007. You're building software that keeps a folder in sync across all your computers. An early version works. Making it reliable for everyone will take a long time.
When you describe it, people shrug. They already email files to themselves or carry USB sticks. How do you find out if people really want it?

options.text: Finish the full product for every computer, then launch
options.feedback: You'd learn the answer for sure, but only after spending a long time on something people might not want.

options.text: Survey people: would you use automatic file sync?
options.feedback: Cheap and fast, but people already told you they're fine with email. Words about a product they can't picture won't tell you much.

options.text: Record a short video of it working and ask viewers to join a waiting list
options.feedback: People see the experience instead of imagining it, and joining the list is a small action you can count. Next card shows what happened.

cards.title: A screencast and a very long line.
body: Drew Houston, Dropbox's co-founder, recorded a simple screencast: his screen, his voice, files appearing on another machine.

A later version was aimed at Digg, a tech news site, and packed with in-jokes for that crowd. By Houston's account, quoted in Eric Ries's *The Lean Startup*, the beta waiting list jumped from about 5,000 to about **75,000** people overnight.

image.label: A waiting list growing from a short line to a huge crowd
image.brief: 왼쪽에 짧은 줄("About 5,000"), 오른쪽에 화면 밖까지 이어지는 긴 줄("About 75,000"). 가운데 재생 버튼 아이콘. 실제 로고나 사이트 이름 표시는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A demo test answers one question.
body: A **demo test** shows the product working, often on video, and asks people to take a small action, like joining a list. It's a form of minimum viable product: the smallest thing that answers your riskiest question.

Dropbox's riskiest question wasn't only "Can we build sync?" It was "Will people care, when they think they already have a solution?" Watching sync happen answered that better than any description could.

cards.title: The video didn't replace building.
body: The story is often told as "make a video instead of a product." That's not what happened. The video showed real, early software. It let people see the experience the finished product promised.
The video tested **demand**. The engineering work tested whether the team could deliver. Dropbox needed both answers, and worked on them side by side rather than one instead of the other.

cards.title: Three conditions made the video powerful.
body: The video wasn't magic. It fit the situation:
list: **Hard to explain, easy to show:** sync sounds dull and looks surprising
**The right audience:** tech fans who felt the pain of scattered files
**A clear next step:** joining a list took seconds and could be counted
cards.callout: Remove any one, and a video tells you much less.

cards.title: A waiting list is not a customer.
body: Joining a list costs a few seconds and an email address. It shows interest, not willingness to pay.

A big list can also hide a narrow audience. Tech fans may love what ordinary buyers ignore. And no video can tell you whether you can deliver at a price that works. Treat sign-ups as permission to test the next assumption, not as proof of a business.

cards.title: Now it's a folding shipping crate.
body: Your small factory has designed a plastic crate that folds flat when empty, saving truck space on return trips. Mass production needs a costly steel mold. You have one hand-built prototype.
Warehouse managers say it "sounds useful." What's your next step?

options.text: Order the mold and start production
options.feedback: You bet the biggest cost on polite interest. If buyers don't order, the mold is money you can't get back.

options.text: Post a demo video of the prototype and count sign-ups
options.feedback: Seeing it fold beats describing it, so you'll learn about interest. But sign-ups are cheap, and a video can't show whether the crate survives real handling.

options.text: Show the prototype on video to buyers, ask for small deposits on a first batch, and stress-test it in a real warehouse
options.feedback: Deposits test commitment, and the warehouse trial tests delivery. It costs more time than a video alone, but it answers both risks before the mold.

cards.softwareNote: The same split applies to apps: a demo video can test whether users want a feature, while a paid pilot and a working prototype test whether they'll pay and whether you can build it.

cards.title: Show it working, then ask for a step that costs something.
body: A demo can prove people want something long before it's finished. It can't prove they'll pay or that you can deliver.
**Try it today:** write down the one assumption your next idea depends on most. Then name the cheapest demo that would let a customer show you, not tell you, that it's true.
